stem: In a hypothetical coding-sequence experiment, investigators remove two nucleotides from the middle of a gene. A second construct instead removes three nucleotides at that position. Translation begins upstream of either deletion. Which of the following best compares the downstream grouping of nucleotides?

options.label: A
options.text: Unchanged before either deletion; undetermined after either deletion
options.explanation: The position of each deletion is known, and codon length is specified by the genetic code. Those facts determine whether downstream triplet grouping changes.
options.misconception: Treats downstream triplet grouping as indeterminate despite knowing both deletion lengths.

options.label: B
options.text: Changed after the two-base deletion; preserved after the three-base deletion
options.explanation: Codons use three nucleotides. Removing two changes the alignment of downstream triplets, whereas removing a complete triplet preserves the reading frame after the deletion.
options.misconception: No misconception: A two-base deletion shifts downstream grouping; a complete-triplet deletion preserves the frame.

options.label: C
options.text: Preserved after the two-base deletion; changed after the three-base deletion
options.explanation: This reverses the effect of deletion size. The nontriplet deletion changes downstream grouping, while deletion of three nucleotides leaves subsequent triplets in the original frame.
options.misconception: Reverses the distinction between deletion lengths divisible and not divisible by three.

options.label: D
options.text: Changed after the two-base deletion; changed after the three-base deletion
options.explanation: Both constructs lose sequence, but sequence loss is distinct from a frame shift. Removing an entire triplet does not change the downstream reading frame.
options.misconception: Assumes every deletion shifts the reading frame, including loss of a complete triplet.

options.label: E
options.text: Preserved after the two-base deletion; preserved after the three-base deletion
options.explanation: The two-base deletion is not divisible by the codon length. Translation continuing across that site therefore groups the downstream bases differently from the original sequence.
options.misconception: Assumes translation retains its original grouping after a deletion shorter than one complete triplet.

context: Learning objective: distinguish a change in codon grouping from loss of sequence within a preserved frame. A nontriplet deletion shifts the downstream reading frame; a triplet-sized deletion preserves the grouping.
